strengths: The paper addresses a realistic and well-motivated problem setting: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data for offline-to-online RL, which prior work has largely ignored (most methods assume curated, reward-labeled, task-specific data).

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive for RL: 72 pixel-based visuomotor tasks spanning DMControl and Meta-World (22 locomotion + 50 manipulation), roughly 12x larger than prior evaluations, with comparisons against training-from-scratch baselines (DrQ v2, Dreamer v3), five offline-data-leveraging baselines (R3M, UDS, RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC), model-based pre-training approaches (iVideoGPT), a diffusion policy imitation baseline, and a continual learning baseline (PackNet).

The diagnosis of why naive world model fine-tuning fails (distributional shift between offline pre-training and online fine-tuning data, illustrated via t-SNE and Wasserstein distances) is a valuable empirical insight and clearly motivates the proposed techniques.

Ablations are thorough: contributions of pre-training, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance are individually dissected (Fig. 6, 11), execution guidance is compared against uncertainty-based reward labeling (OTS), and the role of fine-tuning different world model components is analyzed (Fig. 8).

Reproducibility support is strong: detailed hyperparameter tables, algorithm pseudocode, implementation details including baseline modifications, compute budget reporting (~1728 GPU hours), and full per-task results in the appendix.

The proposed method is architecturally simple (RSSM with zero-padding for action unification, retrieval-based replay, BC prior mixing) yet delivers a substantial 102.8% relative improvement at a 150k sample budget, matching baselines that use 3.5-6.7x more samples.
weaknesses: The individual technical components are relatively incremental: experience rehearsal is essentially retrieval-augmented replay (closely related to RLPD/JSRL-style replay of offline data), and execution guidance is behavior cloning plus a policy-switching schedule reminiscent of JSRL. The novelty lies mainly in combining them with a multi-embodiment world model in the non-curated setting rather than in fundamentally new techniques.

The theoretical analysis in App. B is weak. Proposition 1 effectively assumes its conclusion by constructing D_retrieved such that retrieved states are within epsilon of online states; Proposition 2 is an informal argument; Proposition 3 is a direct application of the TRPO performance-difference lemma under a strong assumption (guide policy uniformly better by delta). These proofs add little genuine insight beyond restating intuition.

The 'non-curated' data is still in-domain and benchmark-specific (collected by unsupervised RL agents on the same DMControl embodiments, and pre-trained RL agents on Meta-World), so the claim of realistic non-curated data is only partially realized; the authors acknowledge this limitation but the positioning sometimes overstates generality.

Only three random seeds per task are used, which is common but limits statistical strength, particularly for high-variance manipulation tasks where confidence intervals in figures are wide and visibly overlapping in places.

Fairness of some baseline comparisons requires scrutiny: baselines like RLPD, ExPLORe, and JSRL-BC cannot natively handle multi-embodiment data and were given preprocessed task-relevant trajectories, and ExPLORe required non-trivial modifications; the paper should more carefully discuss how sensitive conclusions are to these preprocessing choices.

All experiments are in simulation with well-covered benchmarks; no real-robot or in-the-wild data experiments despite motivation emphasizing in-the-wild applicability. Also, tasks in the continual adaptation experiment (Sec. 4.2) are all from the same Ant domain, limiting the strength of the generalization claim.

Some claims could be better supported: the aggregate '102.8% relative improvement' headline number depends on the choice of 150k sample budget, and per-task tables show GSA is weaker than 1M-step baselines on several tasks (e.g., Reach, Cheetah Run variants), which deserves more balanced discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and well-motivated question: how to leverage reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data for efficient online RL, which is more realistic than the curated settings assumed by most offline-to-online RL work.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this area: 72 pixel-based tasks across DMControl and Meta-World, spanning 6 embodiments, with comparisons against training-from-scratch baselines (DrQ v2, Dreamer v3), five offline-data-leveraging baselines (R3M, UDS, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT-style pretraining), a diffusion policy imitation baseline, and a continual adaptation experiment.

The diagnosis of why naive world model fine-tuning fails (distributional shift between offline and online data, illustrated via t-SNE and Wasserstein distance in Fig. 2) is a useful empirical insight and is well supported by the ablations (Fig. 6, 11), which show pre-training alone is insufficient and the two proposed components are complementary.

The two techniques (retrieval-based experience rehearsal and execution guidance via a BC prior) are simple, clearly described, and the full algorithm, hyperparameters, compute budget (1728 GPU hours), and implementation details are provided, supporting reasonable reproducibility.
The continual task adaptation experiment (Fig. 5) demonstrates the method generalizes beyond the standard offline-to-online setup without modification.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (App. B) is weak. Proposition 1 essentially assumes its conclusion: it postulates that retrieved states lie within ε of online states while the rest of the offline data lies at distance ≥ ε, from which the claimed reduction in distribution shift follows trivially. Proposition 2's 'proof' assumes λ is a monotonic function of the retrieval fraction and then argues informally. Proposition 3 is a direct restatement of the TRPO performance-difference lemma under a stated assumption. The theory adds little beyond the empirical claims.

Novelty of individual components is limited: experience rehearsal closely resembles RLPD-style offline replay (the paper's own distinction is retrieval from a much larger non-curated dataset), and execution guidance is a JSRL-style prior-policy switching scheme (the paper acknowledges these similarities). The main contribution is the combination and the setting rather than fundamentally new techniques.

Fairness of comparisons raises concerns: (i) GSA benefits from ~48 GPU-hours of pre-training per task plus a 280M-parameter world model, while the sample-efficiency claims against DrQ v2 / Dreamer v3 count only environment samples and ignore pre-training compute; (ii) baselines are given preprocessed 'task-relevant' offline trajectories, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to this preprocessing choice, which itself requires knowing the target task distribution.

The headline claim that GSA 'matches the performance of baselines trained with substantially more samples' is only partially supported: on DMControl, GSA at 150k (631.1) exceeds Dreamer v3 at 500k (541.8), but on Meta-World, Dreamer v3 at 1M (0.900) substantially outperforms GSA at 150k (0.750). Several individual tasks also regress (e.g., Acrobot Swingup, Cheetah Run, Reach, Pick Place).

Only 3 random seeds per task, and some learning curves (e.g., Assembly, Stick Pull, Dial Turn) show very large variance, making conclusions on the harder manipulation tasks less statistically robust; IQM analysis is only provided for a 6-task subset.

The distributional shift analysis relies on t-SNE visualizations and a Wasserstein distance computed in an unspecified space; a more rigorous characterization of when and why naive fine-tuning fails (e.g., relationship between offline data coverage and fine-tuning success) would strengthen the central claim (C2).

The paper does not explicitly state that code will be released, and the setting is restricted to in-domain, simulation-only data (acknowledged in Limitations), which tempers the significance of the 'non-curated data' framing relative to truly in-the-wild datasets.

strengths: Addresses a realistic and well-motivated problem: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data for offline-to-online RL, which prior offline-to-online methods largely ignore.

Provides a clear empirical diagnosis (distributional shift between offline pre-training and online fine-tuning data, illustrated with t-SNE and Wasserstein distance analysis) that explains why naive world model fine-tuning fails — this analysis is a genuine contribution (C2).

Unusually broad evaluation for an RL paper: 72 pixel-based tasks across DMControl and Meta-World, 12x more tasks than comparable prior work, with full per-task results in the appendix and comparisons against many baselines (DrQ v2, DreamerV3, R3M, UDS, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT, diffusion policy, PackNet).

Thorough ablations isolating each component (pre-training, experience rehearsal, execution guidance), comparison against an OTS-based alternative for exploration guidance, and an analysis of which world model components to fine-tune.
Includes a continual task-adaptation experiment demonstrating the method generalizes beyond the standard offline-to-online setting, and honest limitations discussion.

Strong headline result: 102.8% relative aggregate improvement over from-scratch baselines at 150k samples, and reasonable compute/reproducibility documentation (appendices with code, hyperparameters, GPU hours).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the two core techniques are combinations of existing ideas — experience rehearsal closely resembles RLPD/ExPLORe-style offline replay (with a simple encoder-distance retrieval added), and execution guidance is a variant of JSRL's prior-policy switching. The main novelty is in the setting and the empirical synthesis rather than the method itself.

The 'non-curated' framing is somewhat overstated: the offline data is in-domain, collected by unsupervised RL agents and pre-trained RL agents on the same benchmark suites, with Gaussian noise injected to create mixed quality. This is far from truly in-the-wild data, and the paper acknowledges this only in limitations.

The theoretical analysis (App. B) is weak: Proposition 1 assumes retrieval selects states within epsilon of online states (essentially assuming the conclusion); Proposition 2 is an informal argument rather than a proof; Proposition 3 is a direct application of the TRPO performance-difference lemma with strong assumptions (guide policy better everywhere by delta). The theory adds little support to the empirical claims.

Only 3 random seeds per task, which is thin for RL experiments with the reported variance (wide confidence intervals visible in several figures); some claims of outperforming baselines rest on small margins.

Some headline framing is stronger than the evidence: at 150k, GSA's Meta-World mean (0.750) is comparable to DrQ v2 at 1M (0.753) rather than clearly matching 'larger sample budget' performance in all cases, and GSA underperforms on several individual tasks (e.g., Pick Place, Coffee Pull, Reach, Cheetah Run).

Table 1 claims 'training stability' as a differentiator but this is never substantiated quantitatively; the mid-episode policy switching schedule and retrieval size R are heuristic design choices with limited sensitivity analysis.
Comparison with iVideoGPT and other model-based pre-training baselines relies on numbers from prior papers, raising concerns about setup consistency across environments and evaluation protocols.

strengths: Large-scale, thorough empirical evaluation: 72 visuomotor tasks across DMControl and Meta-World, 6 embodiments, with full per-task results and learning curves in the appendix, which is far more extensive than prior world-model pre-training works that evaluated on a handful of tasks.

Clear and well-motivated problem setting: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment (non-curated) offline data relaxes key assumptions of prior offline-to-online RL methods, and the paper honestly situates its 'non-curated, but in-domain' data relative to in-the-wild data.

Useful diagnostic finding (C2): the analysis that naive world model fine-tuning fails due to distributional shift between pre-training and fine-tuning data, supported by t-SNE visualizations and Wasserstein distance measurements (Fig. 2), is a genuinely informative negative result.

Comprehensive ablations: component-wise ablations (P/ER/G), comparison of execution guidance vs. uncertainty-based reward labeling (OTS), fine-tuning different world model components, retrieval precision analysis, robustness to degraded retrieved data, sensitivity to the guidance schedule, and a DreamerV3 model-size fairness check.

Reasonably fair baseline treatment: baselines like UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, and JSRL-BC are given preprocessed, better-structured (task-relevant) offline data, and NCRL still wins; additional aligned iVideoGPT and DreamerV3 model-size comparisons address fairness concerns proactively.

Practical techniques that are simple and reproducible: retrieval-based experience rehearsal with Faiss, and a BC-based execution guidance schedule that removes JSRL's costly hyperparameter tuning; hyperparameters, algorithm, and compute budget are documented, plus a theoretical section and limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: experience rehearsal is essentially a retrieval-based variant of offline data replay (RLPD/ExPLORe-style), and execution guidance closely mirrors JSRL with mid-episode switching; the paper is a well-engineered combination of known components applied to a new setting rather than a fundamentally new method.

Theoretical analysis is weak: Proposition 1 is nearly circular (it assumes retrieved states satisfy a distance threshold by construction, then concludes retrieved data is closer to online data), and Proposition 2 is a direct restatement of Kakade & Langford (2002); the 'catastrophic forgetting' argument (Definition B.1) is informal and offers no actual proof.

The 'non-curated' data is still author-constructed and in-domain: DMControl data comes from curiosity agents and Meta-World data from noisy TDMPC-v2 agents, so the claimed realism gap relative to curated datasets is narrower than the framing suggests; generalization to new embodiments or in-the-wild data is not demonstrated (acknowledged in Limitations).

Retrieval is based only on the initial observation embedding (Eq. 5) and degrades notably on some tasks (e.g., Door Open precision@500 drops to 68%), and the retrieval hyperparameter k/top-250/500 choice is not ablated; this simple heuristic could be fragile for more diverse datasets.

Some comparisons are somewhat favorable by construction: baseline methods that cannot handle multi-embodiment data receive preprocessed task-relevant trajectories, and iVideoGPT is pre-trained on different data than NCRL; the aligned-setting comparison mitigates but does not fully eliminate dataset asymmetry.

Simulation-only evaluation with a modest number of seeds (3 for baselines vs. 5 for NCRL) and reliance on an older RSSM architecture; results are strong for the tested benchmarks but real-robot and cross-domain transfer claims remain unverified.

Aggregate claims rely on mean scores where a few hard tasks dominate (e.g., Disassemble stays at 0.0; several tasks need larger budgets in Fig. 16), and variance on hard exploration tasks is high, so per-task robustness could be more convincing.

strengths: Large-scale and diverse empirical evaluation: 72 visuomotor tasks across 6 embodiments (DMControl + Meta-World) with reasonable seeds, full per-task result tables, and learning curves in the appendix.

Clear identification and empirical demonstration of an important failure mode: naive world model fine-tuning fails due to offline/online distributional shift, supported by t-SNE and Wasserstein distance analysis (Fig. 2).

Comprehensive ablations isolating the contribution of each component (pre-training, experience rehearsal, execution guidance), plus robustness checks on retrieval quality, annealing schedules, and model-size matching against DreamerV3.

Good breadth of baselines (R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT, DrQ-v2, DreamerV3, PackNet) and an aligned-setting comparison with iVideoGPT that controls for reward shaping and replay pre-filling tricks.
Well-aligned iVideoGPT comparison (Fig. 10) and honest limitations section acknowledging simulation-only evaluation, RNN scaling limits, and in-domain data restrictions.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is essentially DreamerV3 + retrieval-based replay (RLPD-style data sharing) + JSRL-style BC guidance. Both techniques are close to existing work (RLPD, JSRL, UDS), and the paper's contribution is more of an empirical system/integration than a new algorithmic idea.

The 'non-curated' framing is overstated: the Meta-World portion of the offline dataset (50k trajectories) is collected on exactly the 50 downstream tasks being evaluated, so the offline data effectively covers the target task distribution. This weakens the central claim of leveraging task-agnostic data, and the gap to the truly task-agnostic DMControl case is not clearly separated in the results.

The theoretical analysis is weak: Proposition 1 essentially assumes the conclusion (retrieved states satisfy ||s_retrieved - s_on|| < eps while all other states do not), and the forgetting 'proof' is an informal regularization argument; Proposition 2 is a direct re-statement of Kakade & Langford (2002). These add little credibility to the empirical findings.

Evidence for the distributional-shift hypothesis is primarily t-SNE visualizations on a single illustrative task (Shelf Place) and 6 baseline tasks for the Wasserstein figure; a more rigorous quantitative causal analysis (e.g., varying offline/online overlap) would be needed to fully support C2.

Some baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: baselines that cannot handle multi-embodiment data receive 'better-structured' preprocessed data, yet implementation details for the weaker baselines (e.g., the significant modifications to ExPLORe) suggest the comparison may partly reflect tuning effort rather than fundamental method advantages.

Results are heterogeneous across tasks (e.g., Coffee Pull, Reach, Pick Place, Disassemble, Acrobot Swingup Hard where NCRL underperforms), and only 3 seeds for baselines vs 5 for NCRL in the main tables; aggregate claims like 'nearly twice the score' rely on averaging over many easy tasks.

No comparison against obvious ablation-relevant baselines, e.g., simple random-k trajectory replay from the offline data without learned retrieval, which would isolate whether the sophisticated retrieval is actually necessary (Fig. 14 partially addresses this but with a different protocol).

strengths: Thorough and convincing empirical evaluation: 72 visuomotor tasks across 6 embodiments, with 3-5 seeds, confidence intervals, aggregate metrics (IQM, optimality gap), and full per-task results in the appendix.

Careful empirical diagnosis of a genuine failure mode: the paper identifies and visualizes distributional shift between pre-training and fine-tuning data (t-SNE, Wasserstein distances) and shows why naive world model fine-tuning fails, which is a useful finding for the offline-to-online RL community.

Well-executed ablations and robustness analyses: component-wise ablation (P/ER/G), comparison of execution guidance vs. uncertainty-based reward labeling (OTS), sensitivity to the annealing schedule, degradation of retrieved data quality, world model component fine-tuning, and DreamerV3 model-size alignment.

Fair and extensive baseline coverage: training-from-scratch (DrQ-v2, DreamerV3), offline-data methods (R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC), and pre-trained world models (iVideoGPT), including an 'aligned' iVideoGPT comparison that controls for reward shaping and demo replay-buffer tricks.
Detailed continual-task-adaptation experiment (Quadruped) showing NCRL adapts within ~100 trials per task, well beyond PackNet.

Good reproducibility support: complete algorithm, implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute estimates; the problem setting (reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data) is realistic and well motivated.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: both proposed techniques are close to existing ideas — experience rehearsal resembles RLPD-style replay with a retrieval filter, and execution guidance is essentially JSRL with a BC prior and mid-episode switching. The main contribution is the combination and the setting rather than fundamentally new methodology.

The theoretical analysis is weak/near-tautological: Proposition 1 assumes the retrieval criterion it claims to prove the benefit of (states selected by threshold epsilon are declared closer), and Proposition 2 is a direct application of Theorem 4.1 in Kakade & Langford (2002) with mixed-policy substitution. These add little genuine insight.

The Meta-World portion of the offline dataset is collected by TD-MPC2 agents on the same 50 downstream tasks, so the 'non-curated' data contains substantial task-relevant content; retrieval then essentially recovers target-task data. This partially undercuts the claim of leveraging task-agnostic data, and the paper does not systematically test a truly held-out-task regime for the manipulation data.

Retrieval is based only on initial-observation similarity, which can be brittle (precision drops to 68% at top-500 for Door Open); while robustness to degraded retrieval is shown, the design's applicability to tasks where initial observations do not discriminate is unclear.
All experiments are simulation-only, and the data is in-domain; generalization to new embodiments or in-the-wild data is acknowledged but not addressed.
Some baselines (DreamerV3, DrQ-v2) use only 3 seeds, and comparisons to other model-based pre-training methods are limited to the iVideoGPT task set.
